articles.title: Flashy courtship traits tend to evolve faster than combat weapons, study finds
articles.summary: Why do some animal traits change so quickly over evolutionary time? A new study of 531 species suggests decorations used to attract mates tend to evolve faster than weapons used to fight rivals, possibly because mating preferences drift.

articles.title: StructRL: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning with Replay Graphs
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. articles.title: Mind-wandering preserves word-level coupling while disrupting comprehension
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.14814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readers can move their eyes through a page but retain little of its meaning when their minds wander. We tested whether word properties still guide their eyes during these lapses. We analyzed public eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 44 adults who read articles. They marked the text read during each lapse they noticed. We linked these spans to the sentences needed for later comprehension questions. articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? articles.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
articles.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

articles.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
articles.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

articles.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
articles.summary: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.

articles.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
articles.summary: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.
